raw_relations.reason: The contractual term and conditional renewal provision provide the context for the subsequent expiry notices, refused renewal and continued occupation.

The recorded expiry, rejection of renewal and continued occupation supply the factual background for Kasliwal J.'s expired-licensee characterization. They do not independently establish all of its legal consequences.
Kasliwal J. relied on admitted ownership and the pleaded licence relationship when evaluating whether the former licensee could recover possession against the company.
The emergency evacuation and interruption of banking operations form part of the basis for Kasliwal J.'s inference that the bank vacated because of the fire.

Kasliwal J. treated the bank's own request for possession in the 26 May letter as evidence that it had already lost possession. The relation records that interpretation, not an unavoidable inference from the document.

The admitted absence of force in handing over the key was central to Kasliwal J.'s finding that forcible dispossession had not occurred. The remaining unlawful-means question required his further evaluation.
Kasliwal J.'s fire-caused-vacation inference underpins his assessment that the company did not dispossess the bank through force or unlawful means.

The first opinion's inference that the bank vacated because of fire was one substantive reason for the proposed refusal of Section 6 restoration. The proposed disposition is not used to prove the inference.
Kasliwal J.'s assessment that force and unlawful dispossession were absent supports his separately expressed refusal of relief.
The first opinion also relied on the bank's expired-licence status and the company's admitted ownership to justify its proposed disposition.
The company's appellate submissions advanced an interpretation aligned with Kasliwal J.'s absence-of-unlawful-dispossession assessment. The submissions are supporting advocacy, not independent proof.

Company counsel's argument that expiry left the bank without juridical possession corresponded to the status-based reasoning adopted by Kasliwal J. This relation preserves the party-claim attribution.
Ramaswamy J.'s account of a limited repair-related handover challenges the inference that fire-related evacuation necessarily amounted to permanent voluntary loss of possession.

The bank's asserted promise of redelivery provides an alternative explanation of the handover that conflicts with permanent surrender. Its status as a party allegation limits its independent evidentiary force.
Furniture retained inside and the limited description of duplicate-key delivery weaken an automatic inference that the bank abandoned every possessory connection to the premises.
Ramaswamy J. expressly relied on furniture remaining inside the premises when inferring the bank's continuing intention to possess.
The reported redelivery undertaking supports Ramaswamy J.'s interpretation of the bank's intention and the limited purpose of surrender, subject to the unverified status of the alleged promise.
The removal request and the bank's continuing demands for return provide context for Ramaswamy J.'s view that possession remained contested rather than consensually surrendered forever.
The recorded concession directly supports Ramaswamy J.'s conclusion that the company could not subsequently deny dispossession for purposes of the proceeding.
The High Court's adoption of an admitted dispossession date reinforces Ramaswamy J.'s procedural treatment of the concession, without independently authenticating the underlying exclusion.
The reported July dispossession date and August filing support the temporal aspect of Ramaswamy J.'s Section 6 analysis, but timeliness alone does not establish unlawful dispossession.
The High Court's settled-possession finding aligns with Ramaswamy J.'s subsequent analysis. The lower-court conclusion is retained with its separate attribution.
Company counsel's voluntary-surrender argument conflicts with Ramaswamy J.'s conclusion that the earlier concession prevented denial of dispossession in the suit.
Bank counsel expressly advanced the concession-preclusion argument that Ramaswamy J. adopted. The party submission remains distinct from the judicial conclusion.
The bank's argument that its occupation was settled and juridically protected was consistent with Ramaswamy J.'s settled-possession reasoning, though advocacy alone does not establish the facts.
Ramaswamy J.'s treatment of the concession supplied a procedural foundation for proceeding on dispossession and assessing its lack of consent.
His finding of retained intention to possess supported his conclusion that temporary handover did not amount to consent to the later deprivation.
The bank's established settled possession, as characterized by Ramaswamy J., was a central premise of his conclusion that the company could not repossess outside due course of law.

Section 6 supplies the relevant legal conditions of lack of consent and dispossession outside due course of law. The target-case conclusion additionally requires the factual and evaluative premises, not merely the statutory words.
Ramaswamy J.'s broader due-process interpretation connects settled possession and the absence of lawful repossession proceedings to his assessment of the bank's dispossession.
Ramaswamy J.'s separate conclusion concerning dispossession outside due course of law supplied the substantive reason for his proposed dismissal of the company's appeal.
The second opinion's settled-possession finding was an additional substantive reason to uphold restoration, independent of the proposed disposition itself.

Ramaswamy J.'s reservation of contractual classification and refusal to make expired-licence status decisive challenges the weight assigned to that status in Kasliwal J.'s Section 6 analysis. It does not dispute that the bank pleaded a licence.

Ramaswamy J. rejected the implication that dispossession must involve physical force or breach of peace, opposing the narrower evaluation relied upon by Kasliwal J. The disagreement concerns legal significance, not whether physical force was used in transferring the key.

The reported existence of regular proceedings provides procedural context for Ramaswamy J.'s reservation of the lease-versus-licence and underlying-rights controversy, without establishing its merits.
Bank counsel contended that the Section 6 appeal-and-review prohibition restricted Supreme Court review; Ramaswamy J. expressly rejected that contention as applied to Article 136.

Kasliwal J. proposed allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit, whereas Ramaswamy J. proposed dismissing the appeal. The two separate dispositions are incompatible and neither constitutes the Bench's unified merits resolution.

The express larger-bench referral prevents treating Kasliwal J.'s proposed disposition as a completed unified appellate holding. This relation expresses procedural non-resolution rather than contrary factual evidence.
The express larger-bench referral equally prevents treating Ramaswamy J.'s proposed disposition as the completed unified appellate holding.

The High Court's grant of restoration directly contrasts with Kasliwal J.'s proposed reversal. This records disagreement over relief without treating the lower-court decree as independent proof that its reasoning was correct.

coverage_limits: The reconstruction is confined to the complete supplied source for case 1144022, the specified historical judgment and the two registered opinion-specific research translations. No external cases, later judgments or independent legal propositions have been added.
R1 and R2 are scoped RESEARCH_TRANSLATION entries with OPEN_TEXT application, not approved universal legal rules, executable Boolean tests, human gold annotations or legal approval.

The supplied judgment contains two conflicting separate opinions and a final direction to refer the matter for constitution of a larger bench. It does not provide a unified merits determination or a subsequent larger-bench resolution.

Each premise's TRUE state refers to the specifically attributed proposition: a documented statement was reported, counsel advanced an argument, or an identified court or judge expressed a finding. It does not automatically verify the truth of an underlying allegation.

The judgment's reproduction of correspondence, pleadings, contractual terms, the reported key handover and Annexure R is not independent authentication of the original exhibits. The record does not supply separate original documents for verification.

The procedural concession is not automatically evidence establishing each pleaded fact. The source describes its prejudice qualification inconsistently in different passages, and the two opinions differ over its legal effect.

The absence of physical force in the key handover is recorded, while its significance for the later denial of access is disputed. A lack of force is not treated as an automatic negation of dispossession outside due course of law.

Fire-related evacuation, partial handover for repairs, continued retention of belongings, refusal of access and alleged permanent dispossession are kept conceptually distinct. Descriptions of these events by different speakers are not converted into independent duplicate transactions.

The High Court's 19 July 1990 dispossession date is preserved as its reported litigation footing. The first opinion's less precise account of July exclusion is not silently assigned the identical date.

The bank's claimed promise of redelivery is preserved as a PARTY_CLAIM. Ramaswamy J.'s reliance on that account and his separate finding of retained intention to possess are distinguished from independent proof of the undertaking.

Licence expiry, renewal, lease-versus-licence classification, juridical possession, settled possession and entitlement to Section 6 relief are not conflated. Ramaswamy J. reserved the broader contractual classification for regular proceedings.

Section 6's six-month limitation, Government exclusion, restrictions on ordinary appeal or review, and preservation of separate title-based remedies are retained. Ramaswamy J.'s Article 136 analysis is preserved without importing external constitutional doctrine.

The company's reported separate suit and injunctive proceedings are procedural context only. Their subsequent history, outcome and effect on the parties' underlying rights are not established by the supplied material.

The separate dispositions and final referral are included to identify their attribution and procedural limits. Neither individual disposition nor the referral is used as circular evidence proving the substantive premises leading to either opinion.

No burden of proof, unreported witness, missing evidence, assumed identity, additional factual event or later legal outcome is invented. The registry does not separately translate burdens, and unresolved factual or interpretive questions remain open.
